title: Collocation Analysis using R
text:
Goals and Assumptions
Goals


It is not expected that every researchrer writes their own code to calculate association measures
But it is important to understand the algorithmic approach when implementing AMs
This can help to reflect on the various variables and decision points from raw text to measure
This gives also some insights in understanding why some apparently identical procedures may yield different outcomes

Assumptions

Familiar with Chapter 3 of Brezina (2018)
Some experience with any Corpus Lingustics tool (e.g. #LancsBox, AntConc, SketchEngine, WordSmith, …)
Ideally a little exposure to programming

title: Collocation Analysis using R
text:
Why R? - General Remarks



Like in many sciences, tansparency, reproducibility and replication remains a challenge in Corpus Linguistics (Schweinberger, 2026).
Some researchers identify the field as being part of the “replication crisis” (e.g. Sönning & Werner (2021), Schweinberger (2025)).


R, as an open source language with a broad ecosystem, can facilitate transparent research for reproducible results.


This presentation has been created using R, with Positron as IDE (“Integrated development environment”, https://positron.posit.co/) and the publishing system quarto (https://quarto.org/), which allows to have executable code in reports or presentations.

Association Measures and Collocation Frequency
How “sensitive” are common measures towards pure collocation frequency?

title: Collocation Analysis using R
text:
A First Interpretation


Extending the simulation from t-score to other popular measures, we can observe that

z-score and Dice show a very similar distribution. So does MI2 and LogDice
MI, MI2 and MI3 share the same base shape, where the scatter narrows with increasing power
Log-Likelihood looks like a linear relationship with some variation around the regression line
MU and LogRatio seem to have the biggest variation






The scatter plots are created with the same base code as shared in the last meeting, using 10,000 random samples. All plots are build on the same underlying data.

title: Collocation Analysis using R
text:
Measurement Distribution
Normalized between 0 and 1 for all measures.

title: Collocation Analysis using R
text:
Interpretation of AM Distributions


Each association measure transforms the normally distributed co-occurrence sampling in a distinct way:

except of Log Likelihood all measures compress the interquartile range, emphasizing the tails of the distributions (visible as outliers)
MU and MI appear like each other’s invert (but they are not)
The increasing exponents of the numerators in MI, MI2 and MI3 pushes the IQR to the top
Log Dice and _MI3_produce a very similar distribution
Log Ratio keeps the median centered, with almost symmetrical appearance of both ends
z-score and Log Dice both have one prominent outlier

title: Collocation Analysis using R
text:
BNC 1994 Data


Empirical data
A random sample of 150 common nouns from the BNC 1994, stratified by 10 frequency bands. \(\approx 250,000\) node-collocate pairs.


Since we draw from a Zipf-like distribution, the observed frequency effect is less pronounced, but still visible for some measures (notably t-score and MI3).

title: Collocation Analysis using R
text:
BNC 1994 Data - log scale


Empirical data
Using a log-scale for the x-axis gives further insights:

MI3 almost ‘guarantees’ a high score for high cooccurence frequency
many measures show a lower bound with increasing frequency
others, notably MI and Log Ratio converge

title: Collocation Analysis using R
text:
BNC 1994 Data - Boxplot


Empirical data

We see a clear distinction between measures on a standard vs a log scale (with the exception of Log Likelihood)
standard scale: t-score ‘centralizes’ the distribution, whereas MU shows a similar appearance than the observed frequency
Again, z-score and Dice look very similar.
log-scaled measures have their interquartile range below the 0.5 mark, resulting in many outliers in the upper scale
Log Dice is the only measure which produces a significant number of outliers on both ends

And I will love thee still, my dear, while the sands o' life shall run.

And I will come again, my love, thou' it were ten thousand mile."


There are may ways how data can be read into R, and there are methods for basically all common (and uncommon) formats. For Corpus Linguistics data mostly comes as text (.txt) or table (.csv) files.

title: Collocation Analysis using R
text:
Summary Tokenization
Points to Consider
The way tokenization is performed has a significant influence on the association measure results, even for segmented languages like English. Main sources of variation include:


Hyphenated words (e.g. daughter-in-law vs. daughter, in, law)
Multiword expressions (e.g. Supervisory Board vs. Supervisory, Board)
Clitics (That's vs That, 's)
Abbreviations (e.g. U.K. often becomes U, K)



=> Difference in token counts varay across tools and methods used (Brezina & Timperley, 2017). Transparency and consistency is key.

title: Collocation Analysis using R
text:
Determine Tallied Values (1/4)

Most of the values we need can be calculated straightforward from the token vector we have created earlier.
The Number of tokens in the whole corpus, \(N\), equals the number of elements in our vector, which can be derived using the length() function:


# Number of tokens
(N <- length(poem_tokens))

[1] 109



For the frequency of the node (\(R_1\)), we can ask which token is equal to the node, using the expression poem_tokens == "love". Note that == means “equal to” in many programming languages - like a single = in maths. This gives us a logical vecor of TRUE and FALSE’s. Since TRUE corresponds to 1 and FALSE to 0, we can simply sum it up and have the result we need:


# Frequency of node
node <- "love"
(R_1 <- sum(poem_tokens == "love"))

[1] 7

title: Collocation Analysis using R
text:
Determine Tallied Values (2/4)

Likewise for the collocate of interest, \(C_1\):


# Frequency of collocate of interest
collocate <- "my"
(C_1 <- sum(poem_tokens == "my"))

[1] 8



The window size is our choice and depends on the research question.


# Window size
(window_size <- 2)

[1] 2

title: Collocation Analysis using R
text:
Determine Tallied Values (3/4)

For determining the collocation, we need to count - or better make the computer count - not just a sum, but what positional values the node and its collocate has. Usually we want to identify all collocates of our node of interest and how often they occur in our text (corpus).
First, we need to find the positions of our node. We can do so with the function which(). It returns a numeric vector of the node positions in the token vector


# Node positions
(node_positions <- which(poem_tokens=="love"))

[1]   2  16  37  43  72  90 103



Since we decided for a \(L_1\)/\(R_1\) window, we can take the above vector add and subtract 1, respectively, to determine the positions of the co-occurrences:


# get the position numbers of L1 and R1
left_positions <- node_positions - 1
right_positions <- node_positions + 1
# combine the two vectors
all_positions <- c(left_positions, right_positions)

# sort it nicely for us
sort(all_positions)

 [1]   1   3  15  17  36  38  42  44  71  73  89  91 102 104

title: Collocation Analysis using R
text:
Determine Tallied Values (4/4)

Having the numerical values of the collocate positions in the text vector, we can use this as a filter to retrieve the tokens of interest:


(all_collocates <- poem_tokens[all_positions])

 [1] "my"   "my"   "in"   "will" "will" "only" "my"   "is"   "is"   "am"  
[11] "thee" "thee" "and"  "thou"



To summarize this, we apply the table() function:


table(all_collocates)

all_collocates
  am  and   in   is   my only thee thou will 
   1    1    1    2    3    1    2    1    2 



To extract only the numerical value of our collocate of interest, we subset this table using double brackets ([[]]):


(O_11 <- table(all_collocates)[["my"]])

[1] 3

title: Collocation Analysis using R
text:
Compute Observed and Expected

Computing the remaining values for constructing the observed and expected table can be easlily done with applying simple arithmetic:



# remaining observed frequency values
O_12 <- R_1 - O_11
O_21 <- C_1 - O_11
R_2 <- N - R_1
C_2 <- N - C_1
O_22 <- R_2 - O_21




Note: expected frequencies can be calculated with correction for window size or without. Here, we do not correct for window size.




# Calculate expected values without correction
E_11 <- (R_1 * C_1) / N
E_21 <- (R_2 * C_2) / N
E_12 <- (R_1 * C_2) / N
E_22 <- (R_2 * C_2) / N

title: Collocation Analysis using R
text:
MU, MI, Dice, LogRatio
Calculating Association Measures which are based on observed/ecpected frequencies is now straightforward.


MU

(MU <- O_11 / E_11)

[1] 5.839286




MI

(MI <- log2(O_11 / E_11))

[1] 2.545792





Dice

(Dice <- (2 * O_11) / (R_1 + C_1))

[1] 0.4




LogRatio

(LogRatio <- 
  log2((O_11 * R_2) / (O_21 * R_1)))

[1] 3.128105





The formulae of these measures are listed in Section 9.2.

title: Collocation Analysis using R
text:
My reading recommendations

A good starting point to dive deeper into statistics and R for Corpus linguistics is Brezina (2018). This book gives a solid overview about statistical concepts used in the field. Especially on Collocations, see also Brezina et al. (2015).
Also, the work of Stefan Gries in recommended, in particular Gries (2016), which is a good hands-on introduction into R and its application to case studies. A broader focus on linear and mixed models has Gries (2021). Both give a solid and ridgid introduction into working with R in (Corpus) Linguistics.
The Practical Handbook of Corpus Linguistics (Paquot & Gries, 2020) offers an overview on many aspects in Corpus Linguistics research, from corpus compilation to writing a research report. Part II focuses on Corpus methods (with Chapter 7 on Co-occurrence Data, mainly Collocations (Gries & Durrant, 2020)) and Part IV on technical aspects, like programming with R.
There are many other introductions to be considered, for example Bodo Winter (2019). He gives an introduction based on the tidyverse dialect of R (other than Gries, who sticks to base R) before diving into linear models and inferrential statistics. Slightly earlier work of Guillaume Desagulier (2017) but likewise a good introduction to the topic. Please see Kortmann (2021) for further readings.

title: Collocation Analysis using R
text:
Measures Discussed in this Presentation


MU (Evert, 2004)
\(MU = \frac{O_{11}}{E_{11}}\)


(pointwise) Mutual Information (Church & Hanks, 1990)
\(MI = \log_{2}{\frac{O_{11}}{E_{11}}}\)

MI2 (Daille, 1995)
\(MI = \log_{2}{\frac{O_{11}^2}{E_{11}}}\)


MI3 (Daille, 1995)
\(MI = \log_{2}{\frac{O_{11}^3}{E_{11}}}\)

Dice (Smadja, 1993)
\(Dice = \frac{2 \times O_{11}}{R_1 + C_1}\)


LogDice (Rychlỳ, 2008)
\(LogDice = 14 + \log_{2} \frac{2 \times O_{11}}{R_1 + C_1}\)


LogRatio (Hardie, 2014)
\(LogRatio = \log_{2} \frac{O_{11} \times R_2}{O_{21} \times R_1}\)

title: Collocation Analysis using R
text:
Measures Discussed in this Presentation (2/2)


Log-Likelihood (Rayson et al., 2004)
\(LogLikelihood =  2 \times \left( \begin{aligned}
  &O_{11} \times \log(O_{11} / E_{11}) + O_{21} \times \log(O_{21} / E_{21}) \\
  + &O_{12} \times \log(O_{12} / E_{12}) + O_{22} \times \log(O_{22} / E_{22})
\end{aligned} \right)\)

T-score (Stubbs, 1995)
\(t-score = \frac{(O_{11} - E_{11})}{\sqrt{O_{11}}}\)
Z-score
\(z-score = \frac{(O_{11} - E_{11})}{\sqrt{E_{11}}}\)

title: Collocation Analysis using R
text:
Additional Cleaning of Tokenized Text
# Step 1: Concatenate the vector into a single string
poem_string <- paste(poem_tokenized, collapse = " ")

# Step 2: Replace the token "'s" with "is"
poem_string <- gsub("'s\\b", " is ", poem_string)

# Step 3: Remove all punctuation
poem_string <- gsub("[[:punct:]]", "", poem_string)

# Step 4: make all words lowercase
poem_string <- tolower(poem_string)

# Step 5: Split the cleaned string back into a vector of words
# on any white space character as delimiter
poem_tokens <- strsplit(poem_string, "\\s+")[[1]]
